clue.text: Unplaced Texan horse out of the melee almost

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word before it is dropped
the horse sits out, round the outside of what follows, wrapping it up

blocks.note: hoss is the Western drawl for a horse
taken as written, before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A Texan cowboy's horse has bolted from the brawl and ended up nowhere in the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of' looks like leaving the melee, but the horse goes round the outside of it. 'Unplaced' is not a racing result here but a person with no place to live.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without any fixed abode has no place of their own, so 'unplaced' describes a person living rough.

clue.text: Establishment figure on the staff

blocks.note: surface reading: a member of the Establishment employed by some organisation
setter's reading: a printed symbol that establishes the pitch of the lines in music

explanation.surface: A pillar of the Establishment has joined the payroll of some institution.
explanation.walkthrough: The staff is the five-line musical stave, and a clef is the sign at its start that fixes which note each line stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: A clef is the symbol written on a musical stave that establishes the pitch reference for every note after it.

clue.text: Discursive wit restored to the pen

indicators.note: something restored has been put back together, here in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a sty is a pen for pigs

explanation.surface: A writer's rambling humour has been given back to the pen that produced it.
explanation.definitionFit: Discursive talk wanders from topic to topic, taking a winding, meandering course rather than a straight one.

clue.text: Like Tichborne's Orton, one loudly crying out

definitions.note: the answer is the title Orton bore, a noun

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
clamant means clamouring, noisily insistent

explanation.surface: A historical note about the famous Victorian impostor, crying out loudly for his inheritance.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Orton was the Tichborne Claimant, a butcher who in the 1860s posed as the lost heir to a baronetcy. I sits inside CLAMANT, with no word signalling the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Orton laid claim to the Tichborne title and estates, and the Victorian press called him simply the Claimant.

clue.text: Plastic aim destroyed the system? Hardly!

indicators.note: destroyed means broken apart, so the letters before it are smashed and rebuilt

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged
surface padding: an ironic aside that gives no letters

explanation.surface: A protester's slogan: credit-card ambitions have wrecked the economic order, or have they?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardly!' is the setter's wink: plastic credit is the system's lifeblood, not its destroyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Capitalism is the economic order based on private ownership and markets, often simply called the system by its critics.

clue.text: Death-defying 13

blocks.note: surface reading: a reckless stunt that risks life
setter's reading: a gathering whose concentration aims to reach past the grave to the dead

explanation.walkthrough: 13 is FOCUS GROUP; this group focuses on contacting the departed, so it defies death's silence rather than risking a fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritualists sit together at a table hoping to communicate with dead spirits, a group meeting that ignores mortality's barrier.

clue.text: Ape one ahead in this party line diversion

blocks.note: first meaning: copy whoever is in front of you
second meaning: a children's party game played in a line, each copying the one at the front

explanation.surface: Political loyalists slavishly copy their chief, toeing the party line as entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party line' suggests politics and toeing the line, but it is a line of children at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's game has everyone in a queue imitating the actions of the child at the head of the line.

clue.text: Lock out noisy green woodpecker

indicators.note: the lock is placed out, on the outside, enclosing the next part

blocks.note: Yale is a well-known brand of door lock
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A rowdy woodpecker is being locked out of somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird's dialect name imitates its laughing call.
explanation.definitionFit: Yaffle is an old country name for the green woodpecker, echoing its loud laughing cry.

clue.text: See 7
Freewheeling fitness if carbon fuel runs out

indicators.note: when things run out they scatter in all directions, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the chemical symbol for carbon
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cyclist coasting downhill stays fit even when the car's tank has run dry.
explanation.definitionFit: A freewheeling person is independent and unconstrained, relying on nobody else for support.

clue.text: See 10
Championship golfers using clubs or bats in here?

definitions.note: a venue for these golfers, not the golfers
a place, as in the phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: the course near Birmingham that has hosted the Ryder Cup
second meaning: the church tower of the idiom about having bats there, i.e. being crazy

explanation.surface: A sporting question: whether to wield clubs or bats in this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs and bats look like a pair of sports implements; the bats are the flying animals of the saying.
explanation.definitionFit: The Belfry is a famous English golf venue, and a belfry is a bell tower where bats roost in the saying.

clue.text: But does the chattering class come to the point here?

definitions.text: But does the chattering class come to the point here?

blocks.note: surface reading: opinionated media and political commentators who talk endlessly
setter's reading: a panel of ordinary people gathered to discuss a product, supposedly with a sharp concentration

explanation.surface: A sceptic wonders whether the chattering classes ever get to the point.
explanation.walkthrough: The name promises concentration, yet such gatherings are mostly talk, hence the doubting 'But'.
explanation.definitionFit: Market researchers assemble a small panel of people to discuss and react to an idea in a directed conversation.

clue.text: Escapes from the open prisons, say

definitions.text: Escapes from the open prisons, say

blocks.note: surface reading: inmates walking out of minimum-security jails
setter's reading: losses of fluid or gas through a crack, as from anything open or porous

explanation.surface: Prisoners keep slipping away from minimum-security jails.
explanation.walkthrough: An open prison is one with little security; the word for escaping liquid doubles as a figure for people seeping out.
explanation.definitionFit: When fluid or information escapes through a gap, those losses are described as seepage or drips.

clue.text: Such capability restoring Nike''s street cred. O blast!

definitions.note: the answer is the kind of capability, an adjective

indicators.note: restoring suggests rebuilding, so the letters that follow are put together anew
a blast blows things apart, scattering the letters before it

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
St is the abbreviation for street
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sportswear firm's ability to win back its cool image, with a frustrated curse.
explanation.walkthrough: Nike is also the Greek goddess of victory, which fits the nuclear theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-strike capability is a nuclear power's ability to retaliate after surviving an enemy's first attack.

clue.text: Failing to heal bone or scab in such an establishment

definitions.note: describes the kind of workplace, used as an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: the medical term for a fracture whose ends never knit
second meaning: a workplace whose staff are not organised, where a strike-breaker may work freely

explanation.surface: A medical case where a broken bone, or a wound's scab, won't mend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scab' and 'heal' suggest wounds, but a scab is also a strike-breaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons call a fracture that never knits a non-union, and a shop without trade union membership is non-union.

clue.text: See 15
Joe Blogg's morality?

blocks.note: first meaning: the typical ordinary person, Joe Bloggs being the British name for him
second meaning: the medieval English morality play about a man summoned by Death

explanation.walkthrough: Joe Bloggs is the British stand-in name for an average person, like John Doe. A morality was a medieval allegorical drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names both the typical ordinary person and the best-known fifteenth-century English allegorical drama.

clue.text: I'd turn up in "Spanish Eyes", they say, for "These You Have Loved"

indicators.note: they say means the phrase before it is heard rather than read
in a down entry, turning up makes the word read from bottom to top
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: heard as Spanish ayes: the cheers of approval shouted at a bullfight
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A singer would pop up in the hit song Spanish Eyes, played on a nostalgic radio show.
explanation.walkthrough: These You Have Loved was a long-running BBC radio programme of well-loved old music; Spanish Eyes is an old crooner's hit.
explanation.definitionFit: The radio show played familiar favourite records from earlier decades, the kind of tunes people call golden ones.

clue.text: Random numerals open branch briefly with this?

definitions.text: Random numerals open branch briefly with this?

indicators.note: random means in no set order, so the letters that follow are taken in a jumbled sequence

blocks.note: taken as written
BR is the short form of branch

explanation.surface: A bank customer keys in random digits to get into the branch.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a PIN is a set of digits that lets you into your bank account.
explanation.definitionFit: A PIN is a private code of digits issued to one customer, keyed in to access their bank account.

clue.text: Observing one in a slip up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards
in puts the number inside the other word

blocks.note: a lapse is a slip or small error
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is caught watching after a single slip-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Espial is the act of catching sight of or spying on something, a formal noun for watching.

clue.text: See 20
Mole betraying no Scots against us

blocks.note: nae is the Scots word for no
v, versus, means against
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spy turns traitor, refusing the Scots and siding against us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' and 'betraying' paint a spy story, but the mole is a skin blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Naevus is the medical term for a birthmark or pigmented spot on the skin.

clue.text: Are they bound to march by the Foyle?

definitions.text: Are they bound to march by the Foyle?
definitions.note: defines the two-word answer, completed by BOYS at 24

blocks.note: surface reading: certain or obliged to parade
setter's reading: indentured to a master, as trainees once were, and marching in Derry beside its river

explanation.surface: A question whether some group is sure to parade beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Foyle is the river through Derry, Northern Ireland, where a loyalist order named after the youths who shut the city gates in 1688 marches each year.
explanation.definitionFit: The Derry loyal order commemorates young indentured trainees who closed the gates against King James's army.

clue.text: See 22

definitions.note: a cross-reference: the clue for this second word is at 23

blocks.note: surface reading: a pointer to another clue in the grid
setter's reading: the number is misprinted; the clue meant is 23, whose cryptic definition covers both words

explanation.walkthrough: The source prints 'See 22', but this light completes 23-across, which defines the loyal order that marches in Derry each year.
explanation.definitionFit: The second word completes the name of the Derry loyalist marching order commemorating thirteen young trainees of 1688.

clue.text: It's off south-west Scotland: except it's east

blocks.note: but can mean except, as in 'all but one'
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A geography correction: this place lies off the south-west of Scotland, except it is actually east.
explanation.walkthrough: The island lies in the Firth of Clyde, off Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Bute is a small island in the Firth of Clyde, west of the Scottish mainland.

clue.text: But, when entering the ring, one's from Lesotho

indicators.note: entering means one word goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: A boxer from southern Africa climbs into the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: Lesotho was formerly Basutoland, and Basuto is the older name for its people.
explanation.definitionFit: Basuto is the older name for a Sotho person, the people of Lesotho, formerly Basutoland.

clue.text: His career is doubly dangerous

blocks.note: surface reading: a man's job or profession
setter's reading: rushing headlong out of control, a risky movement performed for film at his own risk

explanation.surface: A man whose job is twice as risky as most.
explanation.walkthrough: Career is both a profession and a reckless rush, and he doubles for the star, so 'doubly' works twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A film double performs perilous falls, crashes and chases in place of the star actor.
